description: Equipo conformado por estudiantes de licenciatura del instituto tecnológico de Nuevo leon, formamos un equipo multidisciplinario con habilidades dominadas en diferentes áreas, programación, análisis de datos, manejo de inteligencia artificial, mecatrónica, control, automatización, etc.
summary:
Heliosphere Alert is a free, bilingual (EN/ES) browser game for kids 7–12. It needs no account. Players run a small outpost in Mars’ Jezero Crater with Corvi, a crow astronaut station officer. The challenge asks for real survival trade-offs, and each Sol puts three core resources in tension: oxygen, suit heat and cumulative radiation dose. Going outside to collect science samples costs oxygen and warmth. Making oxygen with MOXIE uses limited solar power. When a solar storm hits, players must drop everything and shelter in a regolith bunker. No choice is free, and missed goals have consequences: Earth’s confidence in the mission drops, and fewer supplies arrive.

Every day is shaped by open NASA data, each piece credited on screen: DONKI space weather (live when it’s available, and clearly labeled when it falls back to the May 2024 storm archive), Curiosity RAD radiation readings, Perseverance MEDA weather and the real Earth–Mars communication delay from JPL ephemerides. Randomized minigames, a rising daily quota and trivia make every run different. Kids don’t memorize facts. They learn what it actually takes to keep humans alive on another world.
details:
What it does and how it works
Heliosphere Alert is a top-down pixel-art survival game that runs in any browser, with no install and no account. Each Sol lasts about 5 minutes. Players leave the base to collect rock, soil, mineral and air samples through science minigames inspired by real Perseverance instruments (SHERLOC, SuperCam, PIXL, MOXIE). Outside, they burn oxygen and suit heat and keep building up radiation dose. Back inside, solar power has to cover the MOXIE oxygen generator, heating and repairs, so every trip outside costs something. Random events like dusty solar panels, a damaged antenna or an incoming CME turn into side missions. A solar storm forces players to race to a shielded regolith bunker. Each morning a transmission from Earth arrives with the real light-travel delay, and the stars of Earth’s confidence rise or fall with how the mission is going. The run ends with a diploma showing how many Sols the player survived.

NASA data
The game uses DONKI space weather (pulled live when available, with an archived May 2024 X-class storm as a clearly labeled fallback), Curiosity RAD radiation, Perseverance MEDA weather, InSight archived science and JPL ephemerides for the communication delay. Every data card shows its source, and archived data is never presented as live.

Benefits and impact
Kids 7–12 learn by deciding, not by reading. They feel why radiation shielding, power budgets and comms delay matter, and they meet real missions and instruments along the way. The game is bilingual (EN/ES) and supports keyboard, mouse and touch, so it reaches Spanish-speaking classrooms and low-end devices.

Tools
Phaser 3, TypeScript, Vite, GitHub Pages, original pixel art with the ENDESGA 32 palette, the NASA DONKI API and NASA open datasets, ElevenLabs for trailer voices, plus automated tests.

Creativity
Corvi, a wise and curious crow astronaut, guides players like a mentor instead of a tutorial. Science minigames get harder each day, a meteor shower marks the change between days, and players can customize their mission patch and accessories. The main intent is that all the data NASA has collected serves a purpose with real parameters of a spatial mission embedded into the game through its APIs

Factors we considered
We designed for the challenge’s rules: 2–3 core resources, no free choices, real consequences, replayability and honest data attribution. We also designed for the age group, with short sessions, readable icons, no violence, no punishing game over (running out of oxygen calls a rescue rocket) and accessible controls.
